summary: Yoho National Park lookout on Tocher Ridge, built in the mid-1960s and in use for about seven years; still standing, reached by a 17.9 km hike with no camping.

facts.design: Based on drawings for a Terra Nova National Park lookout; obliquely sloping windows

access.note: Listed among Parks Canada day hikes. Parks Canada recommends it for very strong hikers only and says camping is not permitted.

visit.trail_note: 17.9 km one way from the Natural Bridge parking area; the last 4.8 km is a steep climb of 915 m. Camping is not permitted.

events.note: Arvid Backman's 1941 report named the ridge a secondary lookout site.
Approximate. The evaluation says the build came about five years after a 1960 review; the blog says the mid-1960s. No exact year found.
The evaluation says the lookout failed to spot the big Amiskwi fire of 1971.
A scouts' project page dated 18-22 July 2000 says a Parks Canada volunteer coordinator offered the scouts the challenge of helping restore the lookout. It does not say what work was done.

evidence.supports: Parks Canada calls it an old fire lookout, reached on a route recommended for very strong hikers, with camping not permitted
evidence.quote: Recommended for very strong hikers only! Follow 12.3 km of riverside trails to the end of the Otterhead Trail (biking permitted up to that point) before you begin the steep hike (4.8 km, 915 m elevation gain) to an old fire lookout. Camping is not permitted!

evidence.supports: Trailhead at Natural Bridge parking area
evidence.quote: Trailhead: Natural Bridge parking area, 4 km west of Field, B.C. on Emerald Lake Road.

evidence.supports: Ridge identified in Arvid Backman's 1941 report as a secondary location
evidence.quote: The Tocher Ridge site was identified as a secondary location in a survey of out of the way places of the park in Arvid Backman's 1941 report.

evidence.supports: Site reconsidered in 1960; about five years later a lookout was built and the Mt. King station closed
evidence.quote: The site was recommenced again in 1960 but it was another five years before action was taken to build a lookout here and close down the station at Mt. King.

evidence.supports: Plans based on drawings for a Terra Nova National Park lookout
evidence.quote: Plans were based on drawings made for a lookout in Terra Nova National Park
This lookout, with its obliquely sloping windows, is the most modern looking of existing lookouts.

evidence.supports: In use for seven years; active lookout before 1972
evidence.quote: because it was only in use for seven years

evidence.supports: Lookout failed to spot the 1971 Amiskwi fire
evidence.quote: The lookout failed to spot the big Amiskwi fire of 1971.

evidence.supports: Metal cladding removed; interior well preserved with furniture from its active days
evidence.quote: much of the original metal cladding has been removed. The interior is well preserved with furniture and equipment left over from its days as an active lookout before 1972.

evidence.supports: Blog says the lookout was built in the mid-1960s and in service for only a few years
evidence.quote: A lookout was finally built in the mid-1960s and was in service for only a few years before abandonment.

evidence.supports: Blog describes the lookout as in excellent condition
evidence.quote: The lookout itself is in excellent condition

evidence.supports: Blog says relics from the lookout days remain inside
evidence.quote: There are many relics and artifacts from the fire lookout days leftover in the tower

evidence.supports: Scouts were offered the restoration challenge by a Parks Canada volunteer coordinator
evidence.quote: Parks Canada Volunteer Coordinator for Yoho, Joe Jazvac, was contacted and he offered the challenge to our boys to help restore this once impressive Fire Lookout

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The evaluation says the lookout was in use for seven years. The blog says a few years. The story gives the evaluation figure and attributes both.

sources.title: Day hikes in Yoho National Park
About Tocher Ridge Lookout (copied heritage notes, author not named)

notes_for_editor: The heritage text (source 2) is an uncredited copy with the note 'Not sure of source' and no date, so its specifics are attributed rather than stated flat. Build year is approximate (1960 review plus about five years, and the blog's mid-1960s); no primary Parks Canada record was found. The 'excellent condition' claim is from an undated blog. The brief's coordinates are a name match to the ridge (CGNDB), not the lookout's own position. A Parks Canada heritage record would settle the build year and the 1971 fire claim.
